query: What sampling frames, choice-set designs, and minimum sample sizes/power calculations are required for DCEs and surveys to credibly estimate awareness, substitution, and welfare responses linked to scanner panels?

response.query: What sampling frames, choice-set designs, and minimum sample sizes/power calculations are required for DCEs and surveys to credibly estimate awareness, substitution, and welfare responses linked to scanner panels?
response.answer: For DCEs and surveys estimating awareness and welfare, use stratified sampling with power analysis; minimum sample size depends on effect size, significance level, and desired power.

results.title: Sample Size Requirements for Discrete-Choice Experiments in Healthcare: a Practical Guide | The Patient - Patient-Centered Outcomes Research | Springer Nature Link
results.content: The purpose of this paper is threefold: (1) to provide insight into whether and how researchers have dealt with sample size calculations for healthcare-related DCE studies; (2) to introduce and explain the required sample size for parameter estimates in DCEs; and (3) to provide a step-by-step guide for the calculation of the minimum sample size requirements for DCEs in health care. That is, we clarified that the following five elements are needed before such a minimum sample size can be determined: significance level (*α*), statistical power level (1−*β*), statistical model used in the DCE analysis, initial belief about the parameter values, and the DCE design. Once the AVC, \( \sum\_{\gamma } \), of the estimated parameters has been established and the confidence level (*α*), the power level (1−*β*), and the effect sizes (*δ*) are set, the minimum required sample size (*N*) for the estimated coefficients in a DCE can be calculated (see Eq. 4).

Title: Sample Size Requirements for Discrete-Choice Experiments in Healthcare: a Practical Guide | The Patient - Patient-Centered Outcomes Research | Springer Nature Link
Although theory exists as to the calculation of sample size requirements for stated choice data, it does not address the issue of minimum sample size requirements in terms of the statistical power of hypothesis tests on the estimated coefficients. The purpose of this paper is threefold: (1) to provide insight into whether and how researchers have dealt with sample size calculations for healthcare-related DCE studies; (2) to introduce and explain the required sample size for parameter estimates in DCEs; and (3) to provide a step-by-step guide for the calculation of the minimum sample size requirements for DCEs in health care. | The minimum sample size needed for a discrete-choice experiment (DCE) depends on the specific hypotheses to be tested. The minimum sample size needed for a discrete-choice experiment (DCE) depends on the specific hypotheses to be tested. In 13 % of the DCE studies (9 of 69 [28:224–31.")–36]), one or more of the following rules of thumb were used to estimate the minimum sample size required: that proposed by (1) Johnson and Orme [37, 38]; (2) Pearmain et al. [39] suggests that, for DCE designs, sample sizes over 100 are able to provide a basis for modeling preference data, whereas Lancsar and Louviere [9:661–77.")] mentioned “our empirical experience is that one rarely requires more than 20 respondents per questionnaire version to estimate reliable models, but undertaking significant post hoc analysis to identify and estimate co-variate effects invariably requires larger sample size”. [6] is not suitable for determining the minimum required sample size for coefficients in DCEs, as this approach focuses on choice probabilities and does not address the issue of minimum sample size requirements in terms of testing for specific hypotheses based on the parameter estimates produced. Statistical power level (1−*β*). Once the AVC, \( \sum\_{\gamma } \), of the estimated parameters has been established and the confidence level (*α*), the power level (1−*β*), and the effect sizes (*δ*) are set, the minimum required sample size (*N*) for the estimated coefficients in a DCE can be calculated (see Eq. 4). *et al.* Sample Size Requirements for Discrete-Choice Experiments in Healthcare: a Practical Guide.

results.content: 1.2 Historical development of sampling methods. 1.3 Types of sampling designs. 1.4 Applications of sampling surveys in various fields. 2.3 Sampling units and sampling errors. 2.4 Comparison of sampling techniques. 3.1 Principles of simple random sampling. 3.2 Methods for selecting simple random samples. 3.3 Estimation and inference in simple random sampling. 3.4 Advantages and limitations of simple random sampling. 4.3 Allocation of sample sizes to strata. 4.4 Analysis and estimation in stratified sampling. 5.1 Principles of cluster sampling. 5.3 Estimation in cluster sampling. 5.4 Efficiency considerations in cluster sampling. 6.2 Probability proportional to size (PPS) sampling. 6.3 Estimation procedures in multistage sampling. 6.4 Applications of multistage sampling. 8.1 Sources of sampling errors. 9.1 Factors affecting sample size. 9.2 Sample size calculation methods. 9.3 Power analysis in sampling. Optimal allocation of resources is crucial for efficient sampling. It involves strategically distributing samples across strata to minimize variance and maximize precision. This approach is key to getting reliable results from sample surveys, a core goal in determining appropriate sample sizes. * Neyman allocation optimizes sample sizes across strata to minimize overall variance. + Allocates more samples to strata with higher variability or larger sizes. - $n\_h$: sample size for stratum h. * Proportional allocation distributes samples proportionally to stratum sizes. + Maintains population proportions in the sample. * Both methods improve precision compared to simple random sampling. * Sampling weights adjust for unequal selection probabilities in complex surveys. + Enables unbiased population estimates from non-proportional samples. * Cost constraints limit the total resources available for sampling. + May vary across strata or sampling units. + Reduces required sample size when sampling fraction is large. ## Sample Size Determination. * Power analysis determines the sample size needed to detect a specified effect. + Smaller effect sizes require larger sample sizes to detect. + Smaller margin of error requires larger sample size. + Higher confidence levels require larger sample sizes. + Corresponds to z-score in sample size calculations (1.96 for 95% confidence). ### Sample Size Calculation. * Sample size formula varies depending on the type of study and parameter of interest. * Factors influencing sample size include. + Study design (simple random sampling, stratified, cluster).
